title: Volumes of Revolution: Disc and Washer Methods
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: A solid of revolution is formed by rotating a flat region about a line called the axis of revolution.
Slicing a solid of revolution perpendicular to its axis gives cross sections that are circles or rings.
Volumes of revolution are a special case of the cross-section formula V = ∫ A dx with circular cross sections.
The radius of a cross section is the distance from the axis of revolution to the edge of the region.
The disc method applies when the region touches the axis, so each cross section is a full disc with no hole.
The disc method gives V = ∫ from a to b of π[r(x)]² dx, where r is the distance from the axis to the curve.
For a region under y = f(x) rotated about the x-axis, the disc radius is r = f(x), the height of the region.
Example: the region under y = √x from 0 to 4 rotated about the x-axis gives V = ∫₀⁴ π(√x)² dx = 8π.
Forgetting the π or failing to square the radius is a common error, since a circle's area is πr².
The washer method applies when there is a gap between the region and the axis, so each cross section is a ring.
A washer has an outer radius R (distance to the far edge) and an inner radius r (distance to the near edge).
The washer method gives V = ∫ from a to b of π([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx.
For a region between an upper curve and a lower curve rotated about the x-axis, R is the upper curve and r is the lower curve.
Example: the region between y = x and y = x² on [0, 1] rotated about the x-axis gives V = ∫₀¹ π(x² − x⁴) dx = 2π/15.
The washer area subtracts the squares of the radii, π(R² − r²), and never the square of the difference π(R − r)².
With R = 3 and r = 2, the true ring area is π(9 − 4) = 5π, while π(R − r)² = π, showing the squares must be taken individually.
For rotation about the y-axis, the radius is a horizontal distance and you integrate with respect to y.
For rotation about a line y = k, the radius is the distance from that line to the curve, such as |f(x) − k|.
Rotating about a horizontal line uses dx with vertical radii; rotating about a vertical line uses dy with horizontal radii.
Disc and washer methods are the cross-section formula with A = πr² or A = π(R² − r²) substituted in.
Setting up the radius correctly as a distance from the axis is where volume-of-revolution problems are won or lost.
Every volume in the unit is an accumulation of infinitesimal slices whose area is integrated, unifying area, cross sections, and revolution.
